n: *Study note:* This lengthy chapter records the mobilization of the troops (vv. {{Numbers 31:1|1-5}}), the war itself (vv. {{Numbers 31:6|6-13}}), the death of the captive women (vv. {{Numbers 31:14|14-18}}), the purification of the nations (vv. {{Numbers 31:19|19-24}}), and the distribution of the spoils (vv. {{Numbers 31:25|25-54}}). For more detail, see G. W. Coats, “Moses in Midian,” *JBL* 92 (1973): 3-10; and W. J. Dumbrell, “Midian—a Land or a League?” *VT* 25 (1975): 323-37.

*Translator's note:* The imperative is followed by its cognate accusative to stress this vengeance. The Midianites had attempted to destroy Israel with their corrupt pagan practices, and now will be judged. The accounts indicate that the effort by Midian was calculated and evil.

*Study note:* The war was commanded by the Lord and was to be divine vengeance on the Midianites. So it was holy war. No Israelites then could take spoils in this—it was not a time for plunder and aggrandizement. It was part of the judgment of God upon those who would destroy or pervert his plan and his people.

*Study note:* This would be the last major enterprise that Moses would have to undertake. He would soon die and “be gathered to his people” as Aaron was.

*Translator's note:* The Niphal imperative, literally “arm yourselves,” is the call to mobilize the nation for war. It is followed by the jussive, “and they will be,” which would then be subordinated to say “that they may be.” The versions changed the verb to a Hiphil, but that is unnecessary: “arm some of yourselves.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “give.”

*Study note:* Some commentators argue that given the size of the nation (which they reject) the small number for the army is a sign of the unrealistic character of the story. The number is a round number, but it is also a holy war, and God would give them the victory. They are beginning to learn here, and at Jericho, and later against these Midianites under Gideon, that God does not want or need a large army in order to obtain victory.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the idiom that these “were in his hand,” meaning that he had the responsibility over them.

*Study note:* It is not clear what articles from the sanctuary were included. *Tg. Ps.-J*. adds (interpretively) “the Urim and Thummim.”

*Study note:* Many modern biblical scholars assume that this passage is fictitious. The text says that they killed every male, but Judges accounts for the Midianites. The texts can be harmonized rather simply—they killed every Midianite who was in the battle. Midianite tribes and cities dotted the whole region, but that does not mean Israel went and killed every single one of them. There apparently was a core of Midianites whom Balaam had influenced to pervert Israel.

*Study note:* Here again we see that there was no unified empire, but Midianite tribal groups.

*Study note:* And what was Balaam doing among the Midianites? The implication is strong. This pagan diviner had to submit to the revealed will of God in the oracles, but he nonetheless could be hired. He had been a part of the attempt to destroy Israel that failed; he then apparently became part of the plan, if not the adviser, to destroy them with sexual immorality and pagan ritual.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “burned with fire.”

*Translator's note:* The ban applied to the encampments and forts of this group of Midianite tribes living in the region of Moab.

*Study note:* This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at {{Numbers 21:1|Num 21:1}}.

*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Again this expression, “the Jordan of Jericho,” is used. It describes the intended location along the Jordan River, the Jordan next to or across from Jericho.
*Translator's note:* The verb is the Piel perfect of the word חָיָה (khayah, “to live”). In the Piel stem it must here mean “preserve alive,” or “allow to live,” rather than make alive.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “every male among the little ones.”

*Study note:* The command in holy war to kill women and children seems in modern times a terrible thing to do (and it was), and something they ought not to have done. But this criticism fails to understand the situation in the ancient world. The entire life of the ancient world was tribal warfare. God’s judgment is poured out on whole groups of people who act with moral abandonment and in sinful pursuits. See E. J. Young, *My Servants, the Prophets*, 24; and J. W. Wenham, *The Enigma of Evil*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “every woman, who is a knower of a man by the bed of a male.”

*Translator's note:* Or “girls.” The Hebrew indicates they would be female children, making the selection easy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who have not known a man’s bed.” The verb יָדָע (yadaʿ) “to know,” “be intimate with,” is used as a euphemism for sexual relations.

*Study note:* Many contemporary scholars see this story as fictitious, composed by the Jews during the captivity. According to this interpretation, the spoils of war here indicate the wealth of the Jews in captivity, which was to be given to the Levites and priests for the restoration of the sanctuary in Jerusalem. The conclusion drawn from this interpretation is that returning Jews had the same problem as the earlier ones: to gain a foothold in the land. Against this interpretation of the account is a lack of hard evidence, a lack which makes this interpretation appear contrived and subjective. If this was the intent of a later writer, he surely could have stated this more clearly than by making up such a story.

*Study note:* These verses are a reminder that taking a life, even if justified through holy war, still separates one from the holiness of God. It is part of the violation of the fallen world, and only through the ritual of purification can one be once again made fit for the presence of the Lord.

*Study note:* Purification by fire is unique to this event. Making these metallic objects “pass through the fire” was not only a way of purifying (burning off impurities), but it seems to be a dedicatory rite as well to the Lord and his people. The aspect of passing through the fire is one used by these pagans for child sacrifice.
*Translator's note:* The idiom here is “take up the head,” meaning take a census, or count the totals.

*Translator's note:* The verb is the Hiphil, “you shall cause to be taken up.” The perfect with vav (ו) continues the sequence of the instructions. This raised offering was to be a tax of one-fifth of one percent for the Lord.

*Study note:* Here again we encounter one of the difficulties of the book, the use of the large numbers. Only 12,000 soldiers fought the Midianites, but they brought back this amount of plunder, including 32,000 girls. Until a solution for numbers in the book can be found, or the current translation confirmed, one must remain cautious in interpretation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who have not known a man’s bed.” The verb יָדָע (yadaʿ) “to know,” “be intimate with,” is used as a euphemism for sexual relations.
*Translator's note:* The word “numbered” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to Moses”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“him”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lifted up the head.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in our hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “our souls.”

*Study note:* The expression here may include the idea of finding protection from divine wrath, which is so common to Leviticus, but it may also be a thank offering for the fact that their lives had been spared.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text does not repeat the word “commanders” here, but it is implied.

*Translator's note:* The purpose of the offering was to remind the Lord to remember Israel. But it would also be an encouragement for Israel as they remembered the great victory.

*Study note:* While the tribes are on the other side of Jordan, the matter of which tribes would settle there has to be discussed. This chapter begins the settlement of Israel into the tribal territories, something to be continued in Joshua. The chapter has the petitions (vv. {{Numbers 32:1|1-5}}), the response by Moses (vv. {{Numbers 32:6|6-15}}), the proposal (vv. {{Numbers 32:16|16-27}}), and the conclusion of the matter (vv. {{Numbers 32:28|28-42}}). For literature on this subject, both critical and conservative, see S. E. Loewenstein, “The Relation of the Settlement of Gad and Reuben in {{Numbers 32:1|Numbers 32:1-38}}, Its Background and Its Composition,” *Tarbiz* 42 (1972): 12-26; J. Mauchline, “Gilead and Gilgal, Some Reflections on the Israelite Occupation of Palestine,” *VT 6* (1956): 19-33; and A. Bergmann, “The Israelite Tribe of Half-Manasseh,” *JPOS* 16 (1936): 224-54.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the place was a place of/for cattle.”

*Text-critical note:* Smr and the LXX have *Sibmah*. Cf. v. {{Numbers 32:38|38}}.

*Translator's note:* Cf. *Baal Meon* in v. {{Numbers 32:38|38}}.
*Translator's note:* The verb is the Hiphil perfect of נָכָה (nakhah), a term that can mean “smite, strike, attack, destroy.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “eyes.”

*Translator's note:* The verb is the Hiphil jussive from עָבַר (ʿavar, “to cross over”). The idea of “cause to cross” or “make us cross” might be too harsh, but “take across” with the rest of the nation is what they are trying to avoid.

*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* The vav (ו) is a vav disjunctive prefixed to the pronoun; it fits best here as a circumstantial clause, “while you stay here.”

*Translator's note:* The preterite with vav (ו) consecutive is here subordinated to the parallel yet chronologically later verb in the next clause.

*Translator's note:* The infinitive construct here with ל (lamed) is functioning as a result clause.

*Translator's note:* The Lord had not given it yet, but was going to give it. Hence, the perfect should be classified as a perfect of resolve.

*Translator's note:* The clause is difficult; it means essentially that “they have not made full [their coming] after” the Lord.

*Translator's note:* The sentence begins with “if they see….” This is the normal way for Hebrew to express a negative oath—“they will by no means see….” The sentence is elliptical; it is saying something like “[May God do so to me] if they see,” meaning they won’t see. Of course here God is taking the oath, which is an anthropomorphic act. He does not need to take an oath, and certainly could not swear by anyone greater, but it communicates to people his resolve.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX adds “those knowing bad and good.”

*Translator's note:* The words “to give” are not in the Hebrew text but have been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of.”

*Translator's note:* The verb is difficult to translate, since it has the idea of “complete, finish” (תָּמָם, tamam). It could be translated “consumed” in this passage (so KJV, ASV); NASB “was destroyed.”

*Translator's note:* The construction uses a verbal hendiadys with the verb “to add” serving to modify the main verb.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you will destroy all this people.”

*Translator's note:* The MT has חֻשִׁים (khushim); the verbal root is חוּשׁ (khush, “to make haste” or “hurry”). But in light of the Greek and Latin Vulgate the Hebrew should probably be emended to חֲמֻשִׁים (hamushim), a qal passive participle meaning “in battle array.” See further BDB 301 s.v. I חוּשׁ, BDB 332 s.v. חֲמֻשִׁים; *HALOT* 300 s.v. I חושׁ, חישׁ; *HALOT* 331 s.v. I חמשׁ.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from before.”
*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* The nuance of the perfect tense here has to be the future perfect.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that which goes out/has gone out of your mouth.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the land is subdued before you.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that which the Lord has spoken to your servants, thus we will do.”
*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the land with its cities in the borders of the cities of the land all around.”
*Study note:* *Havvoth Jair*. The Hebrew name means “villages of Jair.”

*Study note:* This material can be arranged into four sections: from Egypt to Sinai (vv. {{Numbers 33:1|1-15}}), the wilderness wanderings (vv. {{Numbers 33:16|16-36}}), from Kadesh to Moab (vv. {{Numbers 33:37|37-49}}), and final orders for Canaan (vv. {{Numbers 33:50|50-56}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “morrow.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with a high hand”; the expression means “defiantly; boldly” or “with confidence.” The phrase is usually used for arrogant sin and pride, the defiant fist, as it were. The image of the high hand can also mean the hand raised to deliver the blow ({{Job 38:15|Job 38:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes.”
*Text-critical note:* So many medieval Hebrew manuscripts, Smr, Syriac, and Latin Vulgate. Other witnesses have “from before Hahiroth.”
*Translator's note:* *Iim* is a shortened form of the name *Iye-abarim* mentioned in v. {{Numbers 33:44|44}}.

*Study note:* This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at {{Numbers 21:1|Num 21:1}}.

*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text repeats the verb “you will destroy.”

*Study note:* This chapter falls into several sections: the south (vv. {{Numbers 34:1|1-5}}), the west (v. {{Numbers 34:6|6}}), the north (vv. {{Numbers 34:7|7-9}}), the east (vv. {{Numbers 34:10|10-15}}), and then a list of appointed officials (vv. {{Numbers 34:16|16-29}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “command.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this is the land that will fall to you as an inheritance.”
*Translator's note:* The expression refers to the corner or extremity of the Negev, the South.

*Translator's note:* Or “the Ascent of Scorpions” (עַקְרַבִּים [ʿaqrabbim] means “scorpions” in Hebrew).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “its going forth,” or the way it runs.

*Translator's note:* The word for west is simply “sea,” because the sea is west of Israel.

*Study note:* That is, the Mediterranean Sea (also in the following verse).
*Translator's note:* Or “to the entrance to Hamath.”

*Study note:* The word means “harp.” The lake (or sea) of Galilee was so named because it is shaped somewhat like a harp.

*Translator's note:* Or “the Sea of Galilee” (so NLT); NCV, TEV, CEV “Lake Galilee.”
*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* The infinitive forms the direct object of what the Lord commanded. It actually means “to give,” but without an expressed subject may be made passive.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the house of their fathers.” So also a little later in this verse.
*Translator's note:* The verb can be translated simply as “divide,” but it has more the idea of allocate as an inheritance, the related noun being “inheritance.”

*Translator's note:* This sense is created by repetition: “one leader, one leader from the tribe.”

*Translator's note:* The sentence simply uses לִנְחֹל (linkhol, “to divide, apportion”). It has been taken already to mean “allocate as an inheritance.” Here “assist” may be added since Joshua and Eleazar had the primary work.

*Study note:* This section has two main parts, the Levitical cities (vv. {{Numbers 35:1|1-8}}) and the Cities of Refuge (vv. {{Numbers 35:9|9-34}}).

*Study note:* This is the area of the rift valley basin to the north of the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan. See the note at {{Numbers 21:1|Num 21:1}}.

*Translator's note:* The verb is the perfect tense with vav (ו) consecutive: “command…and they will give,” or “that they give.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they”; the referent (the Israelites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “1,000 cubits.” The standard cubit in the OT is assumed by most authorities to be about 18 inches (45 cm) in length, so this would be a distance of 1,500 feet or 500 yards (457.2 meters).

*Translator's note:* The verb is the Qal perfect of מָדַד (madad, “to measure”). With its vav (ו) consecutive it carries the same instructional force as the imperfect.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “2,000 cubits” (also three more times in this verse). This would be a distance of 3,000 feet or 1,000 yards (914.4 meters).

*Study note:* The precise nature of the layout described here is not altogether clear. V. {{Numbers 35:4|4}} speaks of the distance from the wall as being 500 yards; v. {{Numbers 35:5|5}}, however, describes measurements of 1,000 yards. Various proposals have been made in order to harmonize vv. {{Numbers 35:4|4}} and {{Numbers 35:5|5}}. P. J. Budd, *Numbers* (WBC), 376, makes the following suggestion: “It may be best to assume that the cubits of the Levitical pasture lands are cubit frontages of land—in other words on each side of the city there was a block of land with a frontage of 2,000 cubits (v {{Numbers 35:5|5}}), and a depth of 1000 cubits (v {{Numbers 35:4|4}}).”

*Translator's note:* The “manslayer” is the verb “to kill” in a participial form, providing the subject of the clause. The verb means “to kill”; it can mean accidental killing, premeditated killing, or capital punishment. The clause uses the infinitive to express purpose or result: “to flee there the manslayer,” means “so that the manslayer may flee there.”
*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* the verb is the preterite of “die.” The sentence has: “if…he strikes him and he dies.” The vav (ו) consecutive is showing the natural result of the blow.
*Translator's note:* The participle גֹּאֵל (goʾel) is the one who protects the family by seeking vengeance for a crime. This is the same verb used for levirate marriages and other related customs.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text is more vivid: “by lying in wait.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the mouth of”; the metonymy stresses it is at their report.

*Translator's note:* The verb should be given the nuance of imperfect of potentiality.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the priest.” The Greek and the Syriac have “high priest.” The present translation, along with many English versions, uses “high priest” as a clarification.

*Translator's note:* The expression is “the heads of the fathers by the family of the Gileadites.”

*Translator's note:* The Greek and the Syriac add “and before Eleazar the priest.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “heads of the fathers.”
*Translator's note:* The infinitive construct “to give” serves here as the complement or object of the verb, answering what the Lord had commanded Moses.

*Translator's note:* “Men” is understood; it says “to one from the sons of the tribes of the Israelites for a wife,” or if he has her for a wife.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “which they will be to them,” meaning, to those who have them, i.e., the marriages.

*Translator's note:* The verb הָיָה (hayah) is most often translated “to be,” but it can also mean “to happen, to take place, to come to pass,” etc.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the tribe of our fathers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the word that.”

*Translator's note:* The idiom again is “let them be for wives for….”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the one who is good in their eyes.”

*Translator's note:* The subject is “Israelites” and the verb is plural to agree with it, but the idea is collective as the word for “man” indicates: “so that the Israelites may possess—[each] man the inheritance of his fathers.”
*Translator's note:* They married in the family as they were instructed. But the meaning of דּוֹד (dod) is not necessarily restricted to “uncle.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by the hand.”
